mu-935b553f.stem: Which structures pass through the quadrangular space?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
mu-935b553f.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded by teres minor (above), teres major (below), the long head of triceps (medially) and the surgical neck of the humerus (laterally). The circumflex scapular artery passes through the triangular space, and the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery through the triangular interval.

mu-236b2bf7.stem: Which muscles rotate the scapula upwards for abduction of the arm above 90° (elevation)?
options: Trapezius (upper and lower fibres) and serratus anterior
mu-236b2bf7.explanation: Upward rotation of the scapula turns the glenoid fossa upwards. The upper and lower fibres of trapezius and the lower fibres of serratus anterior form a force couple. The rhomboids, levator scapulae and pectoralis minor rotate the scapula downwards.

mu-33a97474.stem: A patient with shoulder pain is asked to place the back of the hand on the lower back and lift the hand away; he cannot (positive lift-off test). Tear of which muscle is suspected?
mu-33a97474.explanation: In the lift-off test the arm is internally rotated, and lifting the hand off the back requires further internal rotation; this is the function of subscapularis. Supraspinatus is assessed with the 'empty can' (Jobe) test, infraspinatus with resisted external rotation.

mu-1879c9ef.explanation: Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve from the posterior cord; with latissimus dorsi it adducts, internally rotates and extends the arm. It is not part of the rotator cuff. Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve.

mu-12097a35.stem: What is the main function of deltoid?
options: To abduct the arm between 15° and 90°
mu-12097a35.explanation: The middle fibres of deltoid are a powerful abductor; the anterior fibres flex and internally rotate, the posterior fibres extend and externally rotate. The muscle is supplied by the axillary nerve, and for intramuscular injection the area about 3–5 cm below the acromion is used.

mu-06f46a27.stem: With the elbow flexed, which is the most powerful supinator of the forearm?
mu-06f46a27.explanation: Because biceps attaches to the radial tuberosity, it supinates very powerfully with the elbow at 90° (the screwdriver movement). With the elbow straight, supination is done mainly by supinator.

mu-99a2d1ae.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord, pierces coracobrachialis, runs between biceps and brachialis and ends in the forearm as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

mu-e916bc04.stem: Which is the main (most powerful) flexor of the elbow joint?
mu-e916bc04.explanation: Brachialis is the 'workhorse' flexor of the elbow in every forearm position; because it attaches to the ulna it is unaffected by forearm rotation. It is supplied mostly by the musculocutaneous nerve, with a small lateral part supplied by the radial nerve.

mu-45622c68.stem: Which spinal segment does the triceps tendon reflex chiefly assess?
mu-45622c68.explanation: The biceps reflex assesses C5–C6 (especially C5), the brachioradialis reflex C6 and the triceps reflex C7 (C6–C8). In a C6–C7 disc herniation (C7 root) the triceps reflex is reduced.

mu-c3f410f3.stem: A 55-year-old man lifting something heavy feels a 'snap' at the front of the shoulder; on bending the elbow a prominent mass forms in the lower front of the arm (Popeye sign). Which structure has torn?
options: Tendon of the long head of biceps brachii
mu-c3f410f3.explanation: The tendon of the long head of biceps can tear from friction and degeneration in the intertubercular sulcus; the muscle belly slides down and forms a mass. Because the short head and brachialis are intact, elbow flexion is not markedly impaired.

mu-56ec334e.stem: What is the order of structures in the cubital fossa from lateral to medial?
options: Brachial artery – biceps tendon – median nerve
Radial nerve – median nerve – brachial artery
Biceps tendon – median nerve – brachial artery
Biceps tendon – brachial artery – median nerve
Median nerve – brachial artery – biceps tendon
mu-56ec334e.explanation: In the cubital fossa, from lateral to medial, lie the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The radial nerve lies deeper and more laterally under brachioradialis. When measuring blood pressure the stethoscope is placed medial to the biceps tendon.

mu-7877f9d2.stem: Between the two heads of which muscle does the median nerve usually pass as it enters the forearm?
mu-7877f9d2.explanation: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres; compression here causes pronator syndrome. The ulnar nerve passes between the two heads of FCU, and the deep branch of the radial nerve through supinator.

mu-b2f28830.stem: Which nerve supplies the part of flexor digitorum profundus going to the 4th and 5th fingers?
options: Main trunk of the median nerve
mu-b2f28830.explanation: FDP has a dual supply: its lateral half to the 2nd and 3rd fingers is supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, its medial half to the 4th and 5th fingers by the ulnar nerve.

mu-e0be960f.stem: After a forearm fracture the patient cannot make an 'OK' sign by touching the tips of the thumb and index finger; because he cannot flex the fingertips, the pulps touch instead of the nail tips. There is no sensory loss. Which nerve is injured?
options: Recurrent branch of the median nerve
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
mu-e0be960f.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve: it supplies FPL, the lateral half of FDP and pronator quadratus. When paralysed, flexion of the distal phalanges of the thumb and index finger is lost; as it has no sensory branch, there is no sensory loss.
